newsitem.title: USA: Steady Fed policy hints markets will set interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Steady Fed policy hints markets will set interest rates.

text.p: The Federal Reserve's decision on Wednesday to keep short-term interest rates unchanged indicates U.S. monetary policy is no longer preemptive and the bond market will be left to set interest rates, analysts said.
However, the central bank might still have adopted, or kept, a bias toward tightening credit during this week's policy-making meeting, they said.
"It's very rare for the Fed to raise rates just once," said William Ford, a former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta.

Under preemptive policies that the Fed adopted in 1994, the central bank tightened credit -- prompting rate hikes for mortgages, car loans, credit cards and other loans -- before inflation had a chance to show up in retail prices.

By leaving the market to set rates, the Fed is now stepping aside and allowing investors to determine how much U.S. Treasury securities are worth, based on the nation's economic outlook, analysts said.

"The Fed has decided that given these ideal conditions of sustained growth with low inflation, they have plenty of time to react to any new development," said David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston. "The Fed is more likely to follow the market than to lead it."
The Fed's Federal Open Market Committee left the federal funds rate at 5.50 percent and the discount rate at 5.00 percent on Wednesday after a two-day meeting.
The central bank last raised the fed funds rate -- which banks charge for overnight loans -- 25 basis points on March 25. It was the Fed's first rate hike in more than two years.
Jones predicted the Treasury market will be prompted to react to U.S. economic data, such as the June payrolls, due for release on Thursday.
Analysts surveyed by Reuters expect a rise of 222,000 in payrolls and a 4.8-percent unemployment rate.
Jones said that in the near-perfect state of the U.S. economy -- a combination of steady growth and low inflation -- "the world of preemptive Fed strikes is over."
Gail Fosler, chief economist at The Conference Board, a private business group, expected U.S. consumer confidence, at its highest since 1969, to reflect a pick-up in economic growth in the fall.
"The growth rate will reaccelerate in the second half of the year. We'll have the same concern in the fall that we had in the spring and the Fed will raise rates again," she said.
"The absence of a Fed move shows the Fed is not against growth, only against inflation," Fosler added.
Fosler explained that policy-makers feel inflationary risks are now so contained that they can resume a preemptive policy at any time without much damage to the economy.

Despite recent signs of deceleration, analysts said the economy might rebound in the second half as businesses continue to invest, manufacturers build up inventories and consumers resume a buying spree after a three-month hiatus.
If true, analysts said the Fed is likely to respond by tightening credit to ward off possible inflationary pressures. The FOMC will meet next on Aug. 19, and then on Sept. 30.

Gross Domestic Product growth is widely forecast to have slowed to somewhere close to 2.0 percent in the second quarter after a red-hot 5.9 percent expansion rate in the first three months of the year.
Analysts said any rebound to economic growth levels above 3.0 percent on a quarterly basis was likely to trigger an interest rate hike.

"You would have to see the economy somewhere above 3.0 percent for the Fed to tighten again. I'm not sure how far above, but it will have to be faster than three," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
Analysts also said that despite the unusually tight labour markets -- latest data put the unemployment rate at 4.8 percent in May -- inflationary wage pressures have been extremely scattered.

"We want the tightest labour market we can get without running any risk of inflation, and maybe we've got that now," said Robert Solow, professor emeritus at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. "It ain't broken, so it shouldn't be fixed."
